k-1.x_notes: Strengths: concrete outline puzzles printed at actual size (sailboat, cat, hexagon, diamond, arrow, star, long hexagon, mountain). All are solvable (I checked that the star takes 3 chevrons, the arrow 2 chevrons and the long hexagon blues). Tracing the pieces is a sensible way for K children to record. Clean header and footer with id. Weaknesses: every task is 'fill this shape', sometimes 'two ways', and nothing more. There is no impossible shape, no fewest-pieces task and no find-all task, so no idea from the outline reaches K-1. Several fills are trivial (2 chevrons in the arrow, 9 greens in the mountain). A K-1 group would probably finish in 20-30 minutes, which is exactly the 'too dumbed down, ends too early' complaint. The labels (Sailboat, Cat, Mountain, First filling) add mild decoration.
k-1.y_notes: Strengths: shared rules stated once, and grid-lined boards printed at actual size. P1 mixes coverable and uncoverable shapes, including an 8-triangle trapezoid that has an even number of triangles and still cannot be covered (5 up, 3 down), with 'say why'. P2 asks for the fewest greens on triangles of side 2, 3 and 4 (answers 2, 3, 4), an entry point to kernel 1. P3 and P6 are find-all tilings (2, 3 and 6, all verified). P4 asks for the fewest blocks (answers 3, 3, 4, all verified and not trivial). P5 is a partner game placing blues, with correct answers 1, 2, 1, 1, 2. That is plenty of varied, real work for 40 minutes. Weaknesses: in P3 and P6 the number of printed copies equals the number of tilings, which gives away the count. The game's 'can always win' question needs adult guidance. The footer has no id.
k-1.reason: Y gives K-1 children real questions (impossible shapes, fewest pieces, all the ways, a strategy game) with enough concrete work to fill the session. X is a short run of plain fill-the-outline puzzles that is likely to run out early and has almost no mathematical idea.

grades-2-3.x_notes: Strengths: a coherent kernel-1 sequence. Triangles of side 2-5 packed with blues lead to 'empty spaces = side length' and why. Six boards are packed first with blues, then with purples, with real contrasts (I verified the empty counts: rhombus 0 vs 4, hexagon 0 vs 2, trapezoid 2 vs 4). It closes with 'cover one purple with blues'. Boards are at actual size. Weaknesses: both impossible boards in P1 have an odd number of triangles (9 and 11), so the key even-area obstruction never appears on a board. The P2 label and text repeat on page 3. Rules are restated in every problem. Recording is fill-in-the-blank ('Blues: __ Empty: __'), and the final question gets one line. Only three problems, which probably fill about 30-40 minutes.
grades-2-3.y_notes: Strengths: rules stated once. P1 includes an even-area impossible trapezoid (7 up, 5 down) and a tileable star. P2 has well-chosen boards with holes: two 'up' holes (impossible), an hourglass that is balanced but whose halves meet only at a point (impossible), and one up plus one down hole (verified tileable). P3 asks for the fewest greens on triangles of side 2-5 with a proof. P4 generalizes to sides 10 and 100. P5 compares chevrons with blues in a table (verified: chevrons never do better). P6 asks the child to invent a 20-triangle board needing at least 6 greens (feasible). P7 asks for the rule for two greens on a side-2 hexagon. I verified the rule exactly: one up and one down always works, two of the same kind never does. Rich, well-sequenced and correct. Weaknesses: heavy on 'explain' prompts and writing for 2nd-3rd graders. P4, P6 and P7 are demanding. The footer has no id.
grades-2-3.reason: Both are sound, but Y puts the up/down obstruction directly on the boards with sharp contrasting examples, then extends to generalizing, inventing a board and finding a rule. X's first problem only shows odd-area failures, and X has fewer, thinner problems.

grades-4-5.x_notes: Strengths: a complete and correct kernel-2 arc on the 1-2-2 hexagon. P1 asks for the 6 tilings, with 8 recording boards and a neat 'line joining the centers' recording method. Six printed flip cards (I verified they are exactly the six LLRR codes) support the flip map, the shortest route A to F (4 flips), the parity question, ribbons, matching codes to tilings, rebuilding a tiling from its ribbon, and flips as adjacent LR/RL swaps. Very concrete, with the board at actual size. Weaknesses: heavily scaffolded into ten small directed steps with fill-in blanks (Route, Code, Card). Page 2 prints all six tilings right after P1 asks the children to find them. P7 states 'two L's and two R's' right after asking how many there are. P10 states the swap rule as a question. Several problems are only a minute or two of work.
grades-4-5.y_notes: Strengths: starts from the same 1-2-2 hexagon, with 10 recording boards and 'explain how you know you have them all'. Then comes the flip map, with 'which two need the most flips'. It moves to the side-2 hexagon (20 tilings) with given pairs that I verified are valid tilings at flip distances 3, 4 and 8, the last being the farthest apart. P4 asks for a 4-flip round trip (one exists) and whether 5 or 7 are possible. P5 defines ribbons with a correct worked example on a different board (LRRLR), so it does not give the answer away. P6 asks for a parity proof and a proof that E to F needs 8. P7 counts the 20 coverings and P8 counts the 20 coverings of a 1-3-3 hexagon. Open, substantive and correct. Weaknesses: demanding for fourth graders. P5 is a long definition, and P6 is a full page of proof lines. Less pre-drawn support than X. The footer has no id.
grades-4-5.reason: Y keeps the investigation open and goes deeper (side-2 hexagon, two ribbons, true lower bounds, counting via ribbons) with correct, well-chosen examples. X is correct and concrete but breaks the discovery into small directed steps and prints its answers.

overall.reason: Y wins every band. Its K-1 pages are substantive and long enough for the session. Its 2-3 and 4-5 pages pose open, well-sequenced problems with carefully chosen contrasting examples, and every answer I checked is correct. X is clean and correct but thin at K-1 and over-scaffolded at 4-5, and Y needs only small edits (footer id, perhaps fewer explain prompts).
